answers.question: Can patients book without creating an account?
answers.answer: Yes. Patients can book as guests without creating an account, providing a name, phone number and email. This was requested in m1 (2 March). In m2 (9 March), the owner initially proposed requiring login to view appointment history, but the final agreement retained guest booking and made login optional. There is no unresolved conflict on this point.

citations.quote: Patients should be able to book an appointment online without creating an account. Just a name, a phone number and an email.
Yes, we talked about guest booking, but now I think patients should log in, so they can see their history.
Could we allow both? Log in if you want, or book as a guest.
Yes, that works. Guests can still book, and patients with an account can see their past appointments.

answers.question: What deposit do new patients pay, and when is it refunded?
answers.answer: New patients pay a $20 deposit; existing patients do not. It is refunded only if they cancel more than 24 hours before the appointment—not exactly 24 hours before or later. This was confirmed in m2 (9 March), resolving m1’s open question about whether to require a deposit.

citations.quote: Yes, we'll take a $20 deposit, for new patients only.
Only if they cancel more than 24 hours before.
Um, I think, maybe a deposit. I'm not sure our patients would like paying up front. We'd have to see.
Okay, I'll note that as an open question. What about cancellations?

answers.question: How did the appointment reminder requirement change across meetings?
answers.answer:
• m1 (2 March): The original requirement was an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (m1:S010).
• m2 (9 March): Front desk reported that many patients preferred email (m2:S010). The owner expanded the requirement to send both: an email two days before and an SMS the day before (m2:S011). Email was added; it did not replace SMS or change its timing.
• m3 (16 March): No further reminder change was recorded. The resulting requirement remains email two days before plus SMS the day before, with no recorded open reminder questions or conflicts.

citations.quote: Patients should get an SMS reminder the day before their appointment.
About reminders. Many patients have told us they prefer email.
Then send both. An email two days before, and the SMS the day before.

answers.question: How will new bookings get into ClinicDesk, and why not through its API?
answers.answer:
New bookings will reach ClinicDesk through a nightly CSV export, using ClinicDesk’s daily CSV import capability—not through its API, because the API is read-only for appointments and therefore cannot create bookings.

This evolved from the owner’s original request in m1 (2 March) for bookings to appear automatically. In m2 (9 March), the developer reported the API limitation. In m3 (16 March), the nightly CSV approach was agreed: “Nightly is fine.” Same-day bookings can be checked in the app rather than waiting for the nightly transfer. This resolved the integration conflict; no open conflict remains.

citations.quote: We use clinic desk for patient records. The bookings should show up there automatically.
I checked clinic desk. They do have an API, but it's read only for appointments.
Clinic Desk can import a daily CSV file. We can export new bookings to it every night.
Nightly is fine. Same day bookings can be checked in the app.

answers.question: Is the waitlist part of the first release?
answers.answer: No. In m2 (9 March), the waitlist was requested but deferred as a candidate for a later release. In m3 (16 March), the owner explicitly confirmed it would be excluded from the first release, and front desk agreed provided it stayed on the list for later. It is deferred, not dropped.

citations.quote: One more thing, we need a waitlist, so if someone cancels, the next person gets offered the slot.
I'll mark the waitlist as a candidate for a later release.
We'll leave the waitlist out of the first release.
That's fine, as long as it's on the list for later.

answers.question: What performance target was agreed for showing available times?
answers.answer: In m3 (16 March), the agreed target was for available times to load in under two seconds on a phone connection. This made the earlier “fast” expectation measurable; the owner confirmed, “Two seconds sounds right.”

citations.quote: On performance, last time we said fast. Can we put a number on it?
The available times load in under two seconds on a phone connection.
Two seconds sounds right.

answers.question: Which accessibility standard should the app meet?
answers.answer: The app should meet WCAG 2.2 Level AA, agreed in m3 (16 March 2026). The analyst proposed that standard, and the owner accepted it.

citations.quote: I'd suggest WCAG 2 .2 level AA, I'll send you a short summary.
Okay, let's go with that.

answers.question: Where must patient data be stored?
answers.answer: Patient data must be stored in Australia. This was confirmed as non-negotiable at the kickoff meeting (m1, 2 March 2026).

citations.quote: Patient information has to stay in Australia. That's non -negotiable.

answers.question: Who asked for staff to be able to block out time slots, and what for?
answers.answer: The front-desk representative asked for staff to be able to block out time slots for staff meetings and leave, at the kickoff meeting (m1).

citations.quote: And we need to block out times ourselves, for staff meetings and leave.

answers.question: Which payment provider will process the deposits?
answers.answer: The meetings do not specify which payment provider will process deposits. In m2, the owner confirmed a $20 deposit for new patients only, but the provider choice is missing.

citations.quote: Yes, we'll take a $20 deposit, for new patients only.

answers.question: What is the launch date for the booking app?
answers.answer: The launch date is not specified in meetings m1–m3. The meetings refer to a “first release,” but do not give a launch date.

citations.quote: We'll leave the waitlist out of the first release.

answers.question: Which requirements changed between the first and second meeting?
answers.answer:
Between m1 (2 March) and m2 (9 March), three requirements were refined and one integration requirement was challenged:

- Accounts and booking: m1 required booking without an account. In m2, the owner initially proposed requiring login, but the final agreement retained guest booking and added optional login, with past-appointment history for account holders. Mandatory login was not the final decision. [m1:S005; m2:S002; m2:S004–S005]
- Deposits: m1 left online deposits as an open question. In m2, this became a definite $20 deposit for new patients only, refundable only when cancellation is more than 24 hours before the appointment. [m1:S012–S013; m2:S007–S009]
- Reminders: m1 specified an SMS the day before. In m2, email two days before was added alongside—not instead of—the day-before SMS. [m1:S010; m2:S011]
- Clinic Desk integration: m1 required bookings to appear automatically in Clinic Desk. In m2, the developer reported that its appointment API was read-only, challenging that requirement. No replacement approach was agreed in m2; options were left for the next meeting. Thus this was an unresolved integration issue at the end of m2, not yet an agreed replacement requirement. [m1:S017; m2:S012; m2:S014]

Separately, m2 introduced a waitlist request, deferred to a later release; it was a new request rather than a change to an m1 requirement. [m2:S015–S017]

answers.question: Who was unsure about requiring patients to log in, and why?
answers.answer: The front-desk representative was unsure about requiring patients to log in during m2 (9 March). They were concerned that many older patients would not want another password. This was in response to the owner proposing login so patients could see their history.

citations.quote: Um? Honestly, I'm not sure about that. A lot of our older patients won't want another password.
Yes, we talked about guest booking, but now I think patients should log in, so they can see their history.

answers.question: Which points in the first meeting did the client leave open, saying they were not sure or would have to check?
answers.answer:
The client left two points open in m1 (2 March):

1. Whether to take online payments/a deposit. The owner said, “Um, I think, maybe a deposit. I'm not sure our patients would like paying up front. We'd have to see.” The analyst explicitly recorded this as an open question. [m1:S011–S013]
2. Whether Clinic Desk had an API. Asked about API availability, the owner replied, “Ah. I believe so. Probably. I'd have to ask them.” Automatic transfer of bookings was requested, but the API’s availability was not confirmed. [m1:S017–S019]

Later resolution: in m2, the deposit became a confirmed $20 charge for new patients only. The Clinic Desk integration requirement changed from automatic booking transfer in m1 to an agreed nightly export in m3. [m2:S007; m3:S002–S003]

Okay, I'll note that as an open question. What about cancellations?

Do you know if Clinic Desk has an API?
Ah. I believe so. Probably. I'd have to ask them.
Yes, we'll take a $20 deposit, for new patients only.
We can export new bookings to it every night.
Nightly is fine.

answers.question: Why did the clinic decide to require every patient to log in?
answers.answer: The clinic did not ultimately decide to require every patient to log in. At m1 (2 March), the owner requested booking without an account. In m2 (9 March), the owner briefly proposed mandatory login so patients could see their history, but later in that same meeting agreed to optional login: guests could still book, while account holders could see their past appointments. The mandatory-login proposal was therefore superseded, not adopted as the final requirement.
